name: Hushai
source_summary: David's loyal friend, called "the Archite," who at David's request pretended to defect to Absalom in order to counter Ahithophel's counsel and secretly relay Absalom's plans back to David.
family_friendly_summary: Hushai was one of David's close and trusted friends. When Absalom rebelled and David had to flee Jerusalem, Hushai wanted to go with him, but David asked him to do something braver instead: return to Jerusalem, pretend to join Absalom's side, and work to give Absalom bad advice that would ruin his plans. Hushai bravely agreed. When Absalom asked for counsel, Hushai argued against the wise advice of Ahithophel, David's former counselor, and convinced Absalom to delay his attack -- giving David crucial time to prepare. Hushai then secretly sent word to David about Absalom's plans through messengers. His loyal, risky mission played a huge part in saving David's kingdom.
adult_story: As David fled Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt, his friend Hushai the Archite came to join him in mourning, but David sent him back with a specific, dangerous assignment: infiltrate Absalom's court and "defeat the counsel of Ahithophel" from the inside (2 Samuel 15:32-34). Hushai presented himself to Absalom as a defector, and though Absalom questioned his sudden loyalty, accepted him into his council (16:16-19). When Ahithophel advised an immediate strike against the fleeing David -- sound counsel that would likely have crushed the rebellion quickly -- Hushai deliberately argued for delay, painting an exaggerated picture of David and his mighty men as ferocious and dangerous, and urging Absalom to gather all Israel first for an overwhelming force (17:5-13). Absalom and his men judged Hushai's counsel better than Ahithophel's, "for the LORD had ordained to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring calamity on Absalom" (17:14). Hushai immediately sent word to the priests Zadok and Abiathar to relay to David, urging him to cross the Jordan without delay (17:15-16), buying David the time he needed to regroup his forces. Hushai's quiet, risky loyalty behind enemy lines proved as decisive to David's survival as any battle fought afterward.
